open_points.subject: release Python patch version
open_points.question: Which exact CPython 3.12 patch release must the assembled release contain?
options: Pin the latest supported CPython 3.12 patch available when the release is assembled.
Pin a patch version selected explicitly in generation inputs.
open_points.default_guess: Pin the latest supported CPython 3.12 patch available at release assembly and record it exactly.
consequences: Selecting at assembly gives current fixes but makes a later assembly with a newer patch a new release.
An explicit generation input maximizes reproducibility but requires someone to maintain the pin.
Accepting any 3.12 patch violates the exact-version release obligation.
open_points.requirement: A release names every dependency it runs with, at an exact version, with its digest: every Python package, direct or transitive, by the digest of its distribution file; the Python version; and the base image of VM Platform's Registry environment by its digest, which fixes the system libraries and the store's engine.

open_points.subject: Registry Linux base image
open_points.text: so is the base image around it — no version named
open_points.question: Which Linux distribution, version and immutable image digest must generation select for Registry?
options: A Debian-based CPython 3.12 image pinned by digest.
An Ubuntu-based image with CPython 3.12 pinned by digest.
Another Linux image whose CPython and required system-library behavior are verified, pinned by digest.
open_points.default_guess: Use a minimal Debian-based CPython 3.12 image pinned by digest.
consequences: A Debian-based image offers broad compatibility at moderate size.
An Ubuntu-based image offers a familiar package base but is generally larger.
Another image may reduce size or change libc and tooling, requiring verification of SQLite, socket and filesystem behavior.
open_points.requirement: A release runs on Linux and on no other host — the kernel that runs Registry's process is Linux's and so is the base image around it — no version named, and its Python is CPython 3.12 (owner, 2026-11-25).

open_points.subject: production Linux kernel selection
open_points.text: the kernel that runs Registry's process is Linux's
open_points.question: Which Linux kernel version or supported kernel range will deployment provide?
options: Pin one kernel version for VM Platform.
Declare and verify a minimum supported Linux kernel version.
Accept any Linux kernel whose required socket and filesystem behavior is available.
open_points.default_guess: Declare a maintained minimum kernel version and pin the production VM to a verified version at or above it.
consequences: One pinned version is reproducible but requires coordinated security upgrades.
A minimum version permits upgrades while requiring compatibility checks.
Accepting any Linux kernel leaves deployment to determine whether the relied-on behavior is actually available.
open_points.requirement: A release runs on Linux and on no other host — the kernel that runs Registry's process is Linux's and so is the base image around it — no version named, and its Python is CPython 3.12 (owner, 2026-11-25).

open_points.subject: filesystems used for the store and backups
open_points.text: Another system, or a Linux or file system on which a call Registry's rules rely on — binding a listener exclusively and to IPv6 alone (A17), renaming a file into place (A17, A18) — does not act as Linux documents it, is unsupported
open_points.question: Which filesystem types and mount arrangements may deployment use for the store and backup locations so that the relied-on rename behavior is supported?
options: Allow a verified set of local Linux filesystems such as ext4 and XFS.
Allow any filesystem after a deployment check proves the required same-filesystem rename behavior.
open_points.default_guess: Use local ext4 filesystems and keep each temporary file in the same filesystem as its rename destination.
consequences: Requiring ext4 gives a narrow, predictable support boundary.
A verified filesystem list gives deployment flexibility but needs compatibility evidence for each entry.
A behavioral check can admit network or unusual filesystems, but the check must faithfully cover the rename guarantees relied upon.
open_points.requirement: Another system, or a Linux or file system on which a call Registry's rules rely on — binding a listener exclusively and to IPv6 alone (A17), renaming a file into place (A17, A18) — does not act as Linux documents it, is unsupported: Registry neither tests for it nor defines what it does there.

open_points.subject: installation rejection on a non-Linux host
open_points.text: Installing a release on a host whose kernel is not Linux's fails, and no instance of it starts (rule 6).
open_points.question: How will installation establish that the host kernel is Linux and prevent Registry from starting otherwise?
options: Have the installer inspect the host kernel before installing or starting the service.
Constrain the deployment platform to Linux and have deployment admission reject every other platform.
Use both an installer preflight and a deployment-platform constraint.
open_points.default_guess: Use both deployment admission and an installer preflight before any Registry process starts.
consequences: Installer inspection makes the refusal explicit but depends on the install entrypoint always being used.
Platform admission centralizes enforcement but requires every deployment path to pass through it.
Both checks provide defense in depth at the cost of duplicated policy.
open_points.requirement: Installing a release on a host whose kernel is not Linux's fails, and no instance of it starts (rule 6).

set_aside.subject: digest identifying the Python runtime
set_aside.text: Installing the release fails when the digest differs for any one dependency of each kind rule 1 names — a direct Python package, a transitive one, the Python version and the base image — and no instance of that release starts.
set_aside.question: What artifact is the authoritative digest-bearing representation of the Python version?
options: Digest the exact CPython distribution archive used to build the runtime.
Digest the installed interpreter package supplied by the base-image distribution.
Digest the installed interpreter binary and its runtime files.
Treat the base-image digest as also proving Python, with no separate Python digest.
set_aside.default_guess: Digest the exact CPython distribution artifact used to build the runtime and record its exact version separately.
consequences: A source-distribution digest identifies build input but does not alone prove the installed binary.
A distribution-package digest follows the base image's package ecosystem and may include downstream patches.
Digesting installed files proves the resulting runtime but requires a canonical file set and hashing procedure.
Relying only on the image digest conflicts with the test's separate Python-version digest check.
set_aside.requirement: Installing the release fails when the digest differs for any one dependency of each kind rule 1 names — a direct Python package, a transitive one, the Python version and the base image — and no instance of that release starts.
